messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj has been a delivery driver for eight years, taking pride in his clean record and his knowledge of every shortcut and back alley in the city. At thirty-four, he and his wife, Priya, were saving for a down payment on a house, a future he felt he was building one successful delivery at a time. He was known for being careful, the kind of driver who always double-checked his mirrors and yielded even when he had the right of way. He saw his caution as a professional skill, a way of protecting himself and others on the busy streets that were his office.

That changed on a rainy Tuesday in October. He was running slightly behind schedule, the wipers struggling to keep up with the downpour that slicked the roads and blurred the streetlights into halos. Turning left onto a residential street, he checked for oncoming traffic and pedestrians. The road seemed clear. As he completed the turn, a teenager on an electric scooter shot out from between two parked cars, hooded and hunched against the rain. Raj slammed the brakes, the van skidding on the wet asphalt, but it was too late. The sickening thud was a sound he would never forget. The boy was thrown from the scooter, his body landing awkwardly on the curb. Raj was out of the van in a second, his own calls to 911 sounding distant and strange to his ears. The police report would later clear him of legal fault, noting the poor visibility and the boy’s unexpected entry into the road, but this offered Raj no comfort.

In the seven months since the accident, Raj’s understanding of himself and his role in the world has calcified into a harsh and unforgiving judgment. He now holds a deep, unshakeable conviction that the event happened entirely because of the way he acted. He has come to believe that a better person, a more attentive driver, would have anticipated the possibility of someone emerging from behind the parked cars. In his mind, he should have protected the boy, and he failed in this fundamental duty. This is not a fleeting thought, but the central truth of his existence now. He lives with the constant, internal refrain that he will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened—for not driving slower, for not seeing the unseen. The self-blame has become a permanent feature of his character, a verdict he has passed on himself from which there is no appeal.

He continues to work, as the bills haven't stopped, but each day is an exercise in quiet agony. Driving the same van, on the same kinds of streets, feels like a cruel pantomime of his old life. He is no longer building toward a future; he is simply going through the motions, weighed down by a guilt that feels as physical as the packages he lifts. His relationship with Priya has grown strained under the weight of his silence. She sees him retreat further into himself, his easy laughter gone, replaced by a constant, weary tension in his shoulders. She tries to reach him, to tell him it wasn't his fault, but her words cannot penetrate the certainty of his own failure. It was her gentle ultimatum—"Raj, I can't watch you disappear. Please, talk to someone"—that finally led him to seek therapy. He sits in the waiting room, not with any real hope for forgiveness, but with a desperate, flickering wish to find a way to carry the person he has become without completely breaking.
